book_understanding.teaching_order: A textbook would define WFPI and CFPI, list their items and weights, then mention their use. Here the video starts from what the learner already owns (WPI and CPI, which contain food), voices the obvious objection (why compute food separately?), answers it twice (narrow scope, then food as the main household expense), and only then builds each basket by taking the food part out of its parent. Weights, formula and use come last. Working from the parent makes each new index a selection to understand rather than a new list to memorise.
book_understanding.breakdown_rule: Each new index is cut as 'parent index minus its non-food parts': first why it is needed, then what goes in (basket by elimination), then how it is weighted and computed, then what it is used for.

narration.density: About 18 terms (WFPI, CFPI, food articles, wide range, food basket, economic well-being, primary articles, manufactured products, fuel and power, six CPI groups, weightage, weighted arithmetic mean, rural/urban/combined, 10 categories, Laspeyres, Paasche, volatility, FCI) in about 330 s of teaching, about 3.3 per minute. Many are recalls from the WPI/CPI videos, so the pace is comfortable for UPSC revision but heavy for class 6-10; the two formula names are dropped in with no explanation.

talmel_summary: Most changes land with their word or up to about 1.5 s before it, and much of the picture writes the speech as labels (full forms, 'food articles are included', group chips, 'weighted arithmetic mean'). The picture truly shows the idea in three places: baskets filled by arrows from the parent's food items, non-food CPI groups struck until only food and beverages remains, and the crowd under the India map turning green for 'economic well-being'. Where the idea is only spoken (formulas, volatility, monthly release, cheap grain for the vulnerable) nothing matching is drawn, and the weights table shows 30 numbers while only one is read.

voice.notes: Calm, even lecture pace in Hinglish with English terms (WFPI, weighted arithmetic mean, categories) read in English. Sets up doubts with a rising 'question yeh hai ki ...' and answers with 'simple sa answer'. Group lists are read quickly in one breath; numbers read as written ('26.14%'). Uses 'yaad kijiye' to recall and 'iska matlab yeh hua' to conclude. No pause or emphasis before the table; ends on a channel plug with no recap.

game_ideas.player_does: drags items out of the WPI goods cart and the CPI trolley (wheat, onion, milk, edible oil, petrol, shirt, house rent, cigarettes, sugar) into the WFPI basket, the CFPI basket or a 'not food' bin
game_ideas.process_happens: a correct food item drops into the matching basket and the basket's weight bar grows by that item's share; a non-food item bounces back with the group it belongs to (fuel and power, housing, pan-tobacco)
game_ideas.win: both baskets hold only food and their weight bars reach 100
game_ideas.lose: if petrol or rent gets into a food basket, a fuel-price shock makes that basket's line jump while food prices are flat: the index stops measuring food
game_ideas.concept: WFPI and CFPI baskets as the food part of WPI and CPI

game_ideas.player_does: acts as the monitoring officer: each month the rural and urban CFPI dials move; when a dial crosses the alarm line the player decides whether to alert FCI
game_ideas.process_happens: an alert sends grain sacks from an FCI godown to ration shops and the plates of poor households refill; a cereal spike pushes the rural dial harder than the urban one because cereals weigh more in the rural basket
game_ideas.win: every spike answered within its month and household plates stay full
game_ideas.lose: ignoring a cereal spike shows rural families cutting meals first, teaching why weights differ by level
game_ideas.concept: monthly monitoring, weights and FCI action

game_ideas.player_does: splits ₹100 of a rural family's and an urban family's food spending across cereals, milk, vegetables, pulses, oils and others
game_ideas.process_happens: the player's split is laid beside the official weights; then a price rise in one item is applied and the two family indices move by different amounts
game_ideas.win: player's split is close to the official pattern (cereals biggest for rural, milk relatively bigger for urban)
game_ideas.lose: giving milk the biggest rural share makes a milk price jump move the rural index more than it really would
game_ideas.concept: CFPI weights by subgroup and level

checks_learned: When a numeric table is shown, every number the learner should keep must be read or visibly pointed to; flag tables where shown numbers outnumber spoken ones by more than 5 to 1.

A named formula or method (Laspeyres, Paasche, weighted arithmetic mean) must appear on screen within about 2 s of being spoken, and should be shown working at least once; flag voice-only formula names.
Flag claims about which formula an official Indian index uses for fact-checking before reuse (here the food indices are said to use Laspeyres and Paasche).
Flag any stretch over 20 s with no canvas change while a new idea is being spoken (270-298 s here).

A sub-index built from a parent should be shown as selection from the parent (arrow from the parent's items into the child's basket, non-members struck); check that the child's elements visibly come from the parent.
The order of labels on screen must match the spoken order (screen R-C-U vs spoken rural-urban-combined).
An outcome claim (index swing passed to FCI, cheap grain for the vulnerable) needs its end shown (grain reaching people), not only the agency's logo.
A transcript gap over 5 s that covers a highlighted item (236-243 s) must be re-transcribed before talmel scoring.

teaching_best.why: the learner's doubt (food is already inside WPI and CPI) is voiced before any definition, so the whole video answers a real question
two-step why: first narrow scope, then food as the biggest household expense leading to economic well-being
each basket is built by elimination from the parent's groups (fuel and power has no food; non-food CPI groups crossed out), which is easy to reason rather than memorise
short cause chain from volatile food prices to monthly release to action by FCI gives the index a purpose

teaching_weak.why: formulas are named in passing ('Laspeyres', 'Paasche') with no explanation or picture; whether Paasche is used for these indices is doubtful
weights are listed but not explained (why cereals weigh more for rural families, milk for urban); only one of the 30 numbers is read
no running example with prices: the index is never computed or shown moving, so 'index' stays abstract
the FCI hand-off and cheap grain are stated as automatic; describe, verify before reuse
ends with no recap of the two baskets
